New FA investment in grassroots still leaves football short-changed

Should probably say upfront that I've met David Conn a few different times, and let's just say that we have extremely different ideas on football and the problems within the grassroot game. I personally believe he's working off of an outdated script, and his views on his Clubs should be ran is both unrealistic and contradictory.

Disclaimer out of the way, he raises a problem here that is definitely worth highlighting and talking about - that is the FA and the Premier League's ability to bamboozle many football fans by providing very little context on their financial outreach programs and the benefits to grassroots. The FA and Premier League are both excellent organisations staffed with talented people, but the money just isn't filtering down and they need to look at themselves in terms of what is the ultimate point of their existence.

The Premier League would have you believe that it is a multinational corporation that just happens to be trading in England. Like a corporation, it takes care of the interests of its shareholders in the Clubs and has to be dragged into spending money on any of the more important social causes. I have to say that they do have a point in terms of how it is not their responsibility to fund grassroots football because they are a business entity who shares its revenues with its members; these members who are regulated by the FA should be the ones improving grassroots in their local area. On the other hand, the reason the league is successful is because of generations of work in grassroots done by coaches and volunteers over the past 100 years - as big as Manchester United are now, they still wouldn't exist if not for a few dedicated volunteers sat in Newton Heath a hundred years ago.

The FA on the other hand is split between two thought processes too. Is the ultimate goal to make the sport more inclusive and throw a wider net for participation, or is the ultimate goal to produce the best players possible? These are not always complimentary and a big issue that I've had with the FA historically is that they seem to bounce between the two depending on the mood of the nation at the time when the strategy documents are being drawn up and presented. If England do well in a tournament like they did in the Women's World Cup then it's time to put more funding into women's football, disabled football, walking football and other schemes attempting to use football as a sporting good for the physical and emotional health of a nation. If England do badly at a tournament like they did at the 2014 World Cup then the mood is that our grassroots need developing by providing a higher standard of coaching to young boys who will then go on to the Premier League and hopefully the England team and the World Cup. The FA tries to do it all and in my opinion their successes are much more based on luck rather than expert guidance.

In a more facts and figures orientated view, this is £60m more than they were previously getting over four years or £15m a year extra. I don't know how much money is needed to take our grassroots game from the current development state it is in to the state that Greg Dyke proclaims that he wants, but I AM sure that that amount is not £15m a year spread across all ages, genders and disabilities. The redundancies for me are not as big an issue as it is for people like Conn because how many people the FA employ is not really a concern and I'm more interested in their funding structures rather than their administrative ones. With that said there are 52 county football associations who themselves are staffed by extremely passionate, underpaid and overworked staff and I have a feeling that many of these redundancies will not be helping them out.

If I was in charge of the FA, I'd personally change numerous things but the first one would be to make people realise that World Cups are not won on pitches - they won in bedrooms when a parent enthusiastically talks and listens to their kid's story about a goal he scored, they're won in back alleys and concrete playgrounds when a kid tries a stepover for the first time and beats his man, and in the media when we infect the adult nation with a football and technical literacy which is passed down through the grassroots and generational structures. In fact the last one is by far the most important of the three and I really do wish that people would understand the importance on the national game that the standard of punditry has in terms of how it becomes a shared intelligence in football supporters and obviously their families, friends and potentially any kids they influence. Under my FA, we'd tie into the BBC or another terrestrial channel and introduce tactical education programs where (ex-)professional managers analysed what was going on in certain games and what they thought about it. This sort of stuff is so important.

On the last point, I totally disagree with his frankly xenophobic attitude to football ownership and don't believe that his concerns are generally reflected in reality. For every Vincent Tan who doesn't give a shit there is a Sheikh Mansour who pumped hundreds of millions into the youth side. And let's not forget that English owners aren't producing players either.
